lessons.title: Factor, cancel and rearrange
knowledge: Factor numerators and denominators before cancelling common factors.
Keep the original excluded denominator values after simplification.
Rearrange by collecting the requested subject; distinguish an identity from an equation.

lessons.title: Solve quadratics and use their roots
knowledge: Solve quadratic equations by factorisation or the quadratic formula, retaining both signs.
Use the sum and product of roots to evaluate symmetric expressions.
Build a quadratic from its roots and check the requested quantity.

lessons.title: Use the quadratic boundary
knowledge: Complete the square with the leading coefficient accounted for.
Use the discriminant to distinguish two distinct, repeated and absent real roots.
Check a parameter value that removes the quadratic term separately.
Identify a quadratic minimum and conditions for positivity or no intersection.

lessons.title: Mark boundaries and test intervals
knowledge: Mark numerator zeros and excluded denominator values before testing interval signs.
Intersect simultaneous inequalities and retain the appropriate endpoints.
Interpret an absolute-value distance bound as an interval.
Do not multiply an inequality by an expression whose sign is unknown.

lessons.title: Use index laws and one common base
knowledge: Use positive-base index laws, including negative and fractional exponents.
Convert powers to a common positive base other than 1 before equating exponents.
Replace a repeated exponential by a positive variable and recover the original input with logarithms.

lessons.title: Combine logarithms before solving
knowledge: State positive logarithm arguments before combining logarithms.
Use product, quotient and power laws to convert a logarithmic equation into a power equation.
Reject candidates outside the original domain and undo any logarithmic substitution.

lessons.title: Find the inner range first
knowledge: Replace an inner function by a variable with its exact attainable range.
Optimise a quadratic on that range by checking admissible vertices and endpoints.
Distinguish an unattained boundary from an attained extreme.
Use the sine/cosine range and the reversed ordering of positive reciprocals.

lessons.title: Sum an arithmetic block
knowledge: Identify the exact first term, last term and inclusive number of terms in an arithmetic block.
Use equal averages of symmetric AP terms and arithmetic sum formulae.
Subtract partial sums to isolate a block; logarithms of powers can reveal an AP of exponents.

lessons.title: Read the ratio before summing
knowledge: Identify the signed common ratio by writing initial terms.
Use finite GP sums, including the ratio-one case, and check absolute ratio below one before summing infinitely.
Powers of GP terms produce corresponding powers of the first term and ratio.
In probability applications, retain the original equally likely sample space when filtering convergence.

lessons.title: Match AP and GP terms before using sums
knowledge: Translate stated AP and GP term positions into equations.
Eliminate the AP difference to determine the GP ratio.
Apply convergence restrictions before using the sum to infinity.

lessons.title: Expand or select the required coefficient
knowledge: An expanded product selects one summand from each bracket.
For one coefficient, enumerate every selection whose powers add to the target, multiply its numerical factors, then add the contributions.
Use binomial coefficients and factorials to count bracket choices.
Track the exponent contributed by a selected term such as x² and keep negative coefficients inside their powers.

lessons.title: Move the input and the height
knowledge: Find transformed points by equating the new inner expression to the old input, then transform the old height.
Interpret translations, stretches and reflections through their effect on input and output.
A negative output multiplier exchanges maxima and minima; successive transformations follow the stated order.

lessons.title: Read a circle from its equation
knowledge: Complete squares in both coordinates to read a circle centre and radius.
Find a circle from diameter endpoints using midpoint and distance.
Distinguish a positive-radius circle, a single point and no real circle from the squared radius.

lessons.title: Update the possible outcomes before dividing
knowledge: Restrict possible outcomes to a given condition before computing a conditional probability.
Update counts on draws without replacement.
Multiply along a probability-tree route and add mutually exclusive routes.

lessons.title: Read the input scale of a trig graph
knowledge: Work with the whole trigonometric input to find periods, zeros and peaks.
Convert radians and degrees and use exact values for standard angles.
Sine and cosine have period 2π and range [−1,1]; tangent has period π and asymptotes π/2+kπ.
Use even cosine and odd sine/tangent symmetry; tangent as sine divided by cosine requires nonzero cosine.

lessons.title: Keep the interval and the original signs
knowledge: Transform the interval along with the trigonometric input and retain every branch in that interval.
Use sin²x+cos²x=1 to reduce an equation to one trigonometric function.
Factor instead of dividing away possible zero factors.
Check original signs after squaring; sqrt(a²)=|a| and denominator exclusions still apply.

lessons.title: Choose a rule and retain both triangles
knowledge: Choose sine or cosine rule according to the known sides and angles.
Retain both valid triangles in an SSA situation and reject degenerate or incompatible candidates.
Use the included angle in the triangle-area formula.
Identify the relevant plane before applying triangle rules in three dimensions.

lessons.title: Rewrite powers before differentiating
knowledge: Rewrite quotients, roots and products as sums of powers before differentiating.
Apply the power rule to rational exponents on the appropriate domain.
Differentiate twice before evaluating a requested second derivative.

lessons.title: Read the shape from derivative signs
knowledge: Factor the derivative and test its sign between zeros and domain breaks.
Use derivative sign changes to classify local maxima and minima.
A zero derivative without a sign change need not be a local extreme.
Use the original function to find stationary-point heights.

lessons.title: Integrate powers, then use the missing information
knowledge: Simplify to powers before integrating and use the power rule except at exponent −1.
Include an integration constant and determine it from an initial value on the same interval; an excluded point can separate intervals with different constants.
Evaluate a definite integral as an antiderivative at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.

lessons.title: Separate signed accumulation from total area
knowledge: Distinguish a signed integral from total geometric area.
Find all intersections and integrate upper minus lower on each separate region.
Split when a curve crosses or an absolute-value formula changes.
The worked absolute-value example treats negative and nonnegative inputs separately.

lessons.title: Turn a ratio into an equation
knowledge: Convert a ratio of quantities into an equation before solving.
Name a repeated exponential as a positive variable to obtain a quadratic.
Reject nonpositive values of the substituted exponential and use its monotonicity to select the largest input.

lessons.title: Simplify lengths before finding an area
knowledge: Simplify square-root lengths using sqrt(z²)=|z| and the sign supplied by the geometric domain.
Express an area as a product of simplified lengths or as an outer area minus pieces.
Cancel shared side or angle factors when taking triangle-area ratios.

lessons.title: Keep every factor in a binomial coefficient
knowledge: Use the complete coefficient nCk·a^(n−k)·b^k in (a+bx)^n.
The combination factor counts which brackets supply bx; powers retain all numerical factors.
Count coefficients by their indices and check end cases separately.
Assess divisibility using prime factors from both the powers and the combination factor.

lessons.title: Count solutions without losing a branch
knowledge: Keep separate branches of a trigonometric equation, including both signs when taking a square root.
Transform the whole input interval and count endpoint solutions carefully.
State the tangent domain and multiply by a denominator only within that domain.
Factor rather than divide by a possibly zero factor, list each branch, and remove duplicate solutions.

lessons.title: Find the allowed range before optimising
knowledge: Replace an inner expression by a variable with its allowed interval before optimising.
Compare both endpoints and any permitted quadratic vertex.
For a^cos(x) with a>0, the extreme values are a and 1/a and their separation is |a−1/a|.
Split the absolute-value equation into cases, multiply by positive a, and retain roots compatible with each case.

lessons.title: Use centres and list the geometry cases
knowledge: Use centre distance and radii to find greatest separation between two circles.
For an unspecified right angle, examine each possible triangle vertex.
Use negative reciprocal gradients for nonvertical perpendicular lines and handle vertical/horizontal lines directly.
Use a quadratic root sum when only the sum is needed, while rejecting degeneracy and duplicates.

lessons.title: Turn repeated areas into a series
knowledge: Read radius squared from completed-square circle equations when only area is needed.
Subtract inner from outer area to express one band.
Recognise an arithmetic progression in successive differences of square areas.
Count the stated bands accurately before summing.

lessons.title: Turn distance into a quadratic
knowledge: Choose the actual optimisation objective, distinguishing height from distance.
Minimise squared distance using both coordinates of the moving point.
Keep the nonnegative range of a squared substitution when minimising the resulting quadratic.
Convert modulus bounds to intervals and check that proposed product extremes can occur together.

lessons.title: Use the two possible triangles
knowledge: Use a common triangle height to turn an area ratio into a side ratio.
Model the two possible side lengths as roots of one cosine-rule quadratic.
Compare root sums/products or subtract Pythagoras equations to eliminate a shared height.
For an acute given angle, compare the opposite side with the perpendicular height and adjacent side to count possible SSA triangles.

lessons.title: Locate the contact point first
knowledge: Name the contact point (p,f(p)) and obtain the tangent gradient from f′(p).
Use the normal gradient and a specified intercept to locate the contact point.
Handle a zero tangent gradient with a vertical normal.
Hold parameters constant during differentiation, then optimise a resulting reciprocal with its sign in view.

lessons.title: Rename a hidden variable
knowledge: Name an entire repeated expression to expose a simpler equation.
State the permitted values of a new squared, logarithmic or reciprocal variable and recover the original variable afterwards.
Write full binomial coefficients and compare their ratios to find a/b without finding both constants.
Distinguish ascending and descending term positions and apply case-defined functions only to allowed inputs.

lessons.title: Count roots from the turning heights
knowledge: Use derivative signs to divide a graph into monotonic pieces.
Evaluate turning heights on the original function to count axis crossings or intersections with a horizontal level.
Count a touching root once and use strict inequalities when distinct roots are required.
Check the positive half of the graph and its height at zero when counting positive roots.

lessons.title: Track the phase of a trig graph
knowledge: Find vertical sine symmetry at input π/2+kπ and cosine symmetry at input kπ.
Translate phase conditions back to x and include negative integers when searching near zero.
For a nonconstant sine or cosine graph with input kx+c and k≠0, use period 2π/|k| and half-period spacing of vertical symmetry axes.
For trig-product inequalities, order zeros, test signs, and add accepted interval lengths.

lessons.title: Recover the totals behind the means
knowledge: Recover totals from means and observation counts.
Track conserved combined totals during a swap and changed counts after removal.
Compute pooled means with correct population weights.
Translate mixture percentages into ingredient amounts.

lessons.title: Move the graph and keep the signed area
knowledge: Track input intervals and output heights through translations and reflections.
Reflecting in y=k sends a height y to 2k−y.
Add or subtract signed integrals over intervals and distinguish them from positive lobe areas.
A vertical constant adds a rectangle; overlapping integrals count some strips repeatedly.

lessons.title: Read the terms before choosing a sum
knowledge: Write initial terms and use the rule to distinguish a geometric progression from a periodic sequence.
A shift of k positions scales an equal-length GP block by r^k.
For an autonomous one-term recurrence u(n+1)=f(u(n)), a repeated value restarts the cycle; a recurrence depending on several terms or on n requires its full state and index phase to repeat.
Count inclusive endpoints, split periodic sums into complete cycles and a remainder, and check infinite-GP convergence.

lessons.title: Simplify surds and rationalise
knowledge: Extract square factors and combine like surds.
Multiply by a nonzero conjugate to rationalise a denominator.
Factor a difference of squares to simplify a surd quotient before calculus.
Keep sqrt(x²)=|x| and all original denominator exclusions.

lessons.title: Divide polynomials and use remainders
knowledge: Divide polynomials by cancelling the highest power, multiplying back and subtracting the full product.
Stop when the remainder degree is lower than the divisor degree.
Evaluate a polynomial at a linear divisor’s zero to find a remainder or test a factor.
Subtract remainder equations to remove unneeded coefficients.

lessons.title: Circle angles, chords and tangents
knowledge: Add the radius at a tangent or the perpendicular from centre to chord to obtain a right triangle.
Apply centre/circumference, semicircle, same-segment, cyclic-quadrilateral and alternate-segment angle results to the correct chord or arc.
Separate internal and external circle-contact cases using centre distance and radii.
Use a right triangle for an internal common tangent of equal circles.

lessons.title: Arcs, sectors and segments
knowledge: Convert angles to radians before using arc length or sector area.
Distinguish sectors from segments and minor regions from major regions.
Find a segment area by subtracting its triangle from a sector.
Trace the complete perimeter, including both arcs and radial gaps in an annular sector.

lessons.title: Vectors and transformations
knowledge: Calculate a displacement vector by subtracting start from finish and combine components.
Use related vectors to establish parallelism or collinearity.
Transform displacement relative to the stated centre for rotations and enlargements.
Apply transformations in order and distinguish length, area and volume scale factors, including negative enlargement factors.

lessons.title: Geometry in three dimensions
knowledge: Identify the relevant cross-section or projected right triangle in a three-dimensional problem.
Compute prism and cylinder volumes and exposed surface areas, omitting shared internal faces.
Find a space diagonal through a face diagonal and measure a line-to-plane angle from its projection.
Read plans/elevations, use scale maps and clockwise bearings, and apply supplied solid formulae.

lessons.title: Use units and measurement bounds
knowledge: Convert both components of compound measures and square or cube length conversions for areas or volumes.
Translate rounded or truncated measurements into intervals with correct endpoints.
Choose quotient or difference bounds using monotonicity and recognise when quantities share the same unknown.
Use significant figures, standard form and estimation to check scale while retaining exact values until needed.

lessons.title: Turn proportion into a multiplier
knowledge: Turn percentage changes into successive multipliers and divide by their product to recover an original amount.
Write direct or inverse proportionality using a fixed constant.
Translate ratios into fractions of a whole and use the correct length, area or volume scale.
Distinguish simple interest, compound growth and the order of deposits or withdrawals.

lessons.title: Read tables and histograms
knowledge: Recover histogram frequencies from bar widths multiplied by density.
Estimate grouped means using midpoints and distinguish grouped estimates from exact summaries.
Find mean, median, mode and range from frequency data.
Select and construct suitable bar, pie, pictogram, two-way, discrete-line, time-series or cumulative displays.

lessons.title: Compare distributions and interpret trends
knowledge: Read quartiles and medians at fractional cumulative counts and interpolate within classes.
Use differences in cumulative frequencies to estimate counts between values.
Compare centre and spread using the same measures and account for extreme values and tail limitations.
Interpret correlation and fitted trends, distinguishing interpolation, extrapolation and causal claims.

lessons.title: Estimate an integral with trapezia
knowledge: Use n+1 heights for n trapezium strips and double only the interior heights.
Compute unequal-width trapezia individually.
Determine over- or underestimation from chord position relative to the curve, rather than increasing/decreasing behaviour.
Track signed approximation error through scaling and constants; recognise an exact semicircle integral geometrically.

lessons.title: Differentiate an accumulated total
knowledge: For a continuous integrand, differentiate an accumulated integral with fixed lower bound and upper endpoint x by evaluating the integrand at x.
Reverse limits when the moving endpoint is the lower one.
Use signed integrals to calculate changes in the accumulated total.
Use integrand signs to classify extrema of the accumulated function and compare endpoints for an absolute maximum.

lessons.title: Read the domain, then AND, OR and NOT
knowledge: Fix the allowed inputs before deciding whether a statement is true.
AND requires both statements; inclusive OR permits either or both; NOT reverses the truth of the whole statement.
Negating a strict inequality includes its equality boundary.
Count whole true statements at the same input when exactly two or exactly one are required.
Some means at least one; not prime is not equivalent to composite because 1 is neither.

lessons.title: Translate IF and ONLY IF before reasoning
knowledge: Identify the premise and conclusion by rewriting a sentence as an if-then implication.
A if B means B implies A; A only if B means A implies B.
If and only if requires both implication directions.
An implication fails precisely when its premise is true and its conclusion false; a false premise is not a counterexample.
A restriction on selected objects need not require any objects to be selected.

lessons.title: Reverse and negate for the contrapositive
knowledge: The converse reverses an implication and needs its own justification.
The contrapositive reverses and negates both clauses and is equivalent to the original implication.
A true premise forces its conclusion, and a false conclusion forces a false premise.
Knowing the conclusion alone does not establish the premise; denying the premise does not deny the conclusion.
Chains of implications can rule out statements as the sole true statement.

lessons.title: Test NECESSARY and SUFFICIENT separately
knowledge: Keep the target fixed: sufficiency tests condition implies target, while necessity tests target implies condition.
Classify a condition by proving each successful direction and giving an allowed counterexample for each failed direction.
Necessary and sufficient describes both directions, as in an if-and-only-if condition.
A stronger condition may be sufficient without being necessary.
For ax+by=c with nonzero coefficients, gradient and intercept signs are determined by -a/b and c/b.

lessons.title: Who is chosen first: EVERY or SOME?
knowledge: Every quantifies over all allowed inputs; there exists requires at least one allowed witness.
Read nested choices in order: a later witness may depend on an earlier input.
One fixed witness working for all inputs is a stronger requirement than choosing a witness separately for each input.
Construct a witness to prove existence and choose a defeating input to disprove a proposed fixed universal witness.
The same existence statement may change truth when its domain changes from integers to reals.

lessons.title: Negate the whole claim, keeping the domain
knowledge: Negate from the outer quantifier inward, swapping every and there exists without changing their order or domains.
The failure of a universal statement is one allowed counterexample; the failure of existence means all allowed candidates fail.
Negating AND gives an OR of negations, while negating OR gives an AND of negations.
To negate an implication, require its premise and the negation of its conclusion.
An if-and-only-if statement fails when exactly one of its two conditions is true; preserve equality when negating inequalities.

lessons.title: Disprove a claim with one allowed example
knowledge: A counterexample must satisfy every hypothesis and violate the conclusion.
For an implication, a true premise and false conclusion are both required.
One counterexample disproves an always-claim, while many successful cases do not prove it.
Check divisibility and primality against their definitions when choosing an integer counterexample.
Negative real inputs can defeat claims that squaring preserves order.

lessons.title: Turn definitions into a direct proof
knowledge: Represent arbitrary even integers as 2k and arbitrary odd integers as 2k+1, with integer k.
Use separate variables for independently chosen integers.
A direct proof begins with the assumptions and uses justified algebra to expose the required form.
To prove divisibility, express the result as the divisor times an integer.
Algebraic representations cover all permitted inputs; numerical tests alone do not.

lessons.title: Cover every case
knowledge: Choose cases that exhaust the stated domain and prove the claim in every case.
Even and odd cases include all integers, including zero and negative integers.
Use |x|=x for x>=0 and |x|=-x for x<0; assign boundary points to a case.
Integer squares leave remainder 0 or 1 modulo 4, as shown by parity cases.
For sums of absolute values, split at each point where an inner expression changes sign.

lessons.title: Assume the opposite and find an impossibility
knowledge: A contradiction proof assumes the denial of the desired conclusion and identifies a precise incompatible fact.
Rationals are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, and division by a nonzero rational.
Use rational closure to prove a rational plus an irrational, or a nonzero rational times an irrational, is irrational.
The impossibility of a negative real square can finish an inequality contradiction.
Showing a numerator and denominator share a factor contradicts rational representation only when lowest terms was assumed.

lessons.title: Put each reason before the step that needs it
knowledge: Order a proof by dependencies: a line may use the hypotheses and previously justified lines.
Introduce symbols before using them and establish nonzero denominators before dividing.
Independent justified lines can sometimes be interchanged.
Translate a logarithm definition into a power and use exponent laws to connect a chain of equalities.

lessons.title: Find the first unsupported step
knowledge: Check each inference using only the assumptions and earlier justified lines, and stop at the first unsupported step.
A true conclusion does not make an invalid or incomplete proof correct.
Circular reasoning assumes the conclusion that the proof is meant to establish.
Dividing by an expression that may vanish can lose a solution; rearrangement and factorisation retain that case.
Squaring is valid forwards, but its candidate roots must be checked in the original equation.

lessons.title: Check what division loses and squaring adds
knowledge: Before cancelling an expression, check and handle the case where it equals zero.
Rearranging to a zero product can preserve solutions that division would discard.
Squaring an equality gives a necessary condition, but the squared equation may contain additional candidate roots.
Substitute candidates back into the original equation, respecting the nonnegative square root.
Equal function outputs need not imply equal inputs, as with squares and supplementary sine values.

lessons.title: Track signs before using an algebraic rule
knowledge: Multiplication or division by a negative number reverses an inequality.
An unknown multiplier sign may require positive, negative and zero cases.
For c>0, |z|>=c means z<=-c or z>=c, including both equality endpoints.
The zero-product rule requires a product equal to zero; a nonzero product does not fix individual factors.
Use the stated signs to bound ratios of negative numbers.

lessons.title: Separate height, gradient and signed area
knowledge: Function value, derivative and integral represent different quantities and must be tested separately.
Adding a constant changes height without changing the derivative.
A zero derivative gives a horizontal tangent and need not give a maximum or minimum.
Check behaviour on both sides before classifying a stationary point.
A zero signed integral can result from cancellation and does not force zero geometric area or a zero function.

lessons.title: Make EVERY input work at the same time
knowledge: Hold the parameter fixed while allowing the input to vary over the whole domain.
Find the most restrictive input to obtain a necessary parameter condition, then prove it sufficient for every input.
Completing the square identifies a quadratic minimum and the input attaining it.
Nonnegativity may allow equality, but a denominator must never vanish.
Expressions sharing an input cannot in general attain their separate minima or maxima simultaneously.

lessons.title: Observe a cycle, then prove the rule repeats it
knowledge: Initial terms suggest a cycle; the recurrence must establish return to the same state.
When a recurrence depends on the index, the index phase must also repeat.
Find a distant term from its position within a proved repeating block.
Compute a long sum using complete blocks and leftover terms.
Repeating terms need not give repeating partial sums when a whole block has nonzero sum; a finite list without a rule does not force its continuation.

lessons.title: Prove a guarantee: first avoid, then force
knowledge: For a required pair sum, partition available numbers into disjoint matching pairs and unmatched singletons.
An avoiding selection takes at most one member per pair and may take all unmatched numbers.
To prove a smallest guarantee, construct a largest avoiding selection and prove one extra choice forces a pair.
Distinctness forbids pairing a number with itself; partners outside the available set do not count.

lessons.title: Test both directions with allowed examples
knowledge: Test sufficiency and necessity as separate implications, using allowed counterexamples for directions that fail.
A sorted odd-length list has a middle entry; an even-length median averages the middle two entries.
Repetitions may make an even-length median an entry, while distinctness changes that conclusion.
Do not add assumptions such as positive, distinct or nonzero unless stated.
Apply the direction tests to divisibility, equations, inequalities and logarithmic conditions.

lessons.title: Make every and there exists do real work
knowledge: Prove existence by constructing a witness; test universal statements with troublesome allowed inputs.
A nonconstant real linear expression can attain any real value; when its coefficient vanishes, inspect the constant separately.
An input-dependent witness differs from one fixed choice that must work for every input.
A parameter stays fixed during a universal test, which includes negative inputs, zero and large magnitudes when the domain is all reals.
Negate nested every/exists claims by reversing quantifiers in place and preserving each domain.

lessons.title: Check the argument, not just the conclusion
knowledge: Locate the first inference not supported by earlier proof lines.
A true one-way implication does not establish its converse; even a true converse needs justification.
A polynomial having no real linear factors does not imply that its integer values are prime.
Squaring gives candidates that require substitution into the original equation.
Cancellation requires a nonzero factor; rational closure can supply the contradiction in irrationality proofs.

lessons.title: Find the largest selection that avoids a pair
knowledge: Use the actual available numbers to form disjoint pairs with the target sum.
With p pairs and s unmatched numbers, the largest pair-free choice has p+s elements; if a pair exists, one more forces it.
Prove minimality with an explicit avoiding selection as well as the forcing bound.
A missing partner or forbidden self-pair leaves a number unmatched.
An arithmetic-progression sum formula does not solve an arbitrary-selection guarantee question.

lessons.title: Collect all contributions to a coefficient
knowledge: To find a coefficient in a product, list every pair of exponents whose sum is the target exponent.
Multiply the matching coefficients and add all contributions.
The coefficient of x^k in (1+x)^n is the binomial coefficient n choose k.
Substituting x=1 sums all coefficients; it gives one target coefficient only when the contributing terms exhaust that whole row.
For a constant term with positive and negative powers, require the total exponent to be zero.

lessons.title: Use the interval before comparing values
knowledge: Establish an ordering throughout the allowed interval before applying an outer function.
On 0<x<1, x^2<x<sqrt(x).
An exponential base greater than 1 preserves exponent order, while a base between 0 and 1 reverses it.
For continuous functions on [a,b] with a<b, strict pointwise ordering throughout (a,b) gives the same strict ordering of their integrals from a to b.
Read |x-a| as distance from a; midpoint boundaries solve comparisons of distances and intersections of their solution intervals.

lessons.title: Keep the same input when finding extremes
knowledge: Find extrema of a sum using the same input or row for every term; separate extrema may be unattainable together.
The sum of separate maxima is an upper bound, but claiming a maximum also requires an allowed input attaining it.
Complete the square for a sum of quadratics rather than adding separate minima.
Carry the full range through each stage of a composition, checking turning points inside the interval.
Squaring an interval containing zero gives minimum zero and a maximum from its largest absolute endpoint.
Use sine and cosine ranges and monotonicity on the actual intermediate intervals to bound nested trigonometric functions.

lessons.title: Use geometry to test a universal claim
knowledge: Translate a geometric condition into lengths, areas or angles before deciding what it forces.
Triangle area with two sides and the included angle is half the product of the sides and the sine of that angle.
For angles strictly between 0 and 180 degrees, equal sine allows equal or supplementary angles.
A nonsquare rectangle inscribed in a circle gives equal centre-to-side triangle areas without regularity.
A symmetric example proves possibility, while a universal symmetry claim needs proof or an allowed irregular counterexample.

lessons.title: Combine conditions before choosing
knowledge: Exactly one requires one entire statement to hold and all others to fail.
Use shared inputs and implications between listed statements to exclude statements that would force another truth.
Equivalent statements, including a statement and its contrapositive, have matching truth values.
A guarantee over a larger input set implies the same guarantee over each contained smaller set.
An iff fails in the two cases where exactly one component is true; different false universal rules may fail at different inputs.
After identifying the sole possible true rule, construct a consistent example if needed.

lessons.title: Complete each stage of a proof
knowledge: Existence needs an allowed solution; uniqueness needs proof that every solution equals that candidate.
A necessary candidate condition must be completed by substitution in the original problem or by reversible steps.
A contradiction proof retains the original assumptions, denies the target and finishes with explicitly incompatible facts.
Order definitions and conditions before proof lines that use them.
Rewrite logarithm definitions as powers and regroup exponents to connect a longer chain without assuming its conclusion.
Equal products do not force equality of corresponding factors.

lessons.title: Integer cases and supplied definitions
knowledge: Cover every possible remainder modulo a positive integer to prove a divisibility or remainder claim.
A prime divisible by another prime must equal that prime, so check the prime itself before declaring a multiple composite.
Products of consecutive integers provide small factors; divisibility by 2 and 3 ensures divisibility by 6, but overlapping factors cannot be counted twice.
For a supplied definition, preserve the order of member, factor and partner choices, allowing later choices to depend on earlier ones.
Negating every member has a suitable choice means one member has no suitable choice.
Keep other-member restrictions explicit: self-divisibility cannot supply a different partner.

lessons.title: Use an identity at useful inputs
knowledge: An identity holds at every allowed input; useful substitutions can make function arguments coincide or produce simultaneous equations.
Opposite heights equally spaced around a centre imply a zero value at that centre and signed integral cancellation on intervals with that midpoint.
Symmetry about one centre does not guarantee cancellation on an interval with a different midpoint.
Write the transformed input for each graph operation, then compare the two operation orders.
An identity f(x+T)=f(x) establishes a period, not necessarily the smallest positive period; positive integer multiples are also periods.
Replacing x by -x reflects roots and exchanges their positive and negative signs.

lessons.title: Find the full parameter range
knowledge: Check parameter values at which an equation changes degree before using a quadratic discriminant or dividing by a coefficient.
A nondegenerate quadratic has two distinct real roots for positive discriminant and one distinct repeated root for zero discriminant.
The substitution u=x^2 retains u>=0: positive u gives two real x values, zero gives one and negative u gives none.
Two distinct positive roots of the quadratic in u are needed for four distinct real roots of an even quartic; use discriminant, root sum and product.
Use cubic turning heights to classify real-root counts and inspect zero turning heights at parameter boundaries.
Prove the full necessary-and-sufficient range; a narrower sufficient condition alone does not describe all successful parameters.

lessons.title: Prove a bound and attain it
knowledge: An extremal solution requires a bound excluding every better value and a construction attaining that bound.
Round a lower bound on an integer count upward, then check that the proposed arrangement works.
Circular chair coverage requires checking the wrap-around gap as well as internal gaps.
Sort data to use medians, range and mean constraints; bound the total in terms of the median and then build an attaining list.
For a sorted triple with mean mu and median m, the two outer entries sum to 3mu-m.
Distinctness applies across the full construction, including separate triples; case splits can be needed to prove the least overall range.

lessons.title: Justify what a recurrence preserves
knowledge: Prove that a recurrence update preserves a property, then use the initial state to justify repeated application.
The update (x,y) to (y,x+y) preserves the full set of common divisors by addition forwards and subtraction backwards, so adjacent HCFs agree.
A property proved for adjacent terms need not hold for separated terms.
A two-term recurrence needs a repeated ordered pair to restart the process; repeating parity states need not mean repeating numerical values.
Prove that an interval bound survives the next update to control distant terms without a closed formula.
Separate a non-repeating start from a later cycle and count from the actual cycle start; periodic sums still require leftover-block checks.

lessons.title: Test claims about whole functions
knowledge: A functional counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis everywhere on the required domain or interval.
Increasing function height does not imply increasing gradient, and positive height does not imply positive gradient.
An integral of a square is nonnegative, while an ordinary signed integral may cancel.

On a nonempty forward interval, subtract shared integration intervals to isolate a sign constraint; for a continuous function, a nonpositive integral forces at least one nonpositive value, not nonpositivity everywhere.
The distinct roots of a product are the combined roots of its factors, with overlaps counted once.
A nonzero cubic has opposite-sign tails and cannot be positive on the entire real line.

lessons.title: Compare events before counting
knowledge: Event inclusion gives a non-strict probability inequality; strictness requires a positive-probability outcome in the larger event but outside the smaller.
Equal probabilities do not imply equal events.
For conditional probability with equally likely outcomes, first restrict to outcomes consistent with the given information.
Count an at-least-one event through its complement to avoid multiple counting; independent trials permit multiplying complementary probabilities.
Sampling without replacement is generally dependent.
A swap pairing proves that half of arrangements place one distinct object before another; fix prescribed positions before counting remaining arrangements.
A minimum overlap follows from excess memberships, and an explicit allocation proves it attainable.

additionalConcepts.title: Calculate with signed numbers and fractions
knowledge: Place value determines a digit’s contribution; compare signed numbers on a number line, where the number further right is larger.
Subtracting a negative adds its positive value; multiplication or division of two numbers with the same sign is positive, and with different signs is negative.
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, use a common denominator when adding or subtracting, and divide by a nonzero fraction by multiplying by its reciprocal.
Work through brackets, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right.
A reciprocal is \(1/a\) for \(a\ne0\); squaring and cubing mean repeated multiplication, while cube roots reverse cubing, so \(\sqrt[3]{-8}=-2\).

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · M2.1, M2.2, M2.4, M2.6, M2.10

example.question: Evaluate \((-1\tfrac12+\tfrac34)\div(-\tfrac38)\).
steps: Convert the mixed number: \(-1\tfrac12=-\tfrac32=-\tfrac64\).
Calculate the bracket: \(-\tfrac64+\tfrac34=-\tfrac34\).
Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal: \(-\tfrac34\times(-\tfrac83)=2\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A minus sign before a mixed number applies to the whole number: \(-1\tfrac12=-\tfrac32\), not \(-\tfrac12\).

additionalConcepts.title: Read algebraic notation and substitute carefully
knowledge: Adjacent symbols mean multiplication: \(3ab^2=3\times a\times b\times b\), whereas \(a+b\) is a sum.
Terms are joined by addition or subtraction; factors are multiplied, and only terms with identical variable parts can be collected.
An expression has a value, an equation states an equality to solve, a formula relates quantities, an identity holds for every allowed input, and an inequality compares values.
Substitute each given value in brackets before evaluating powers, especially when the value is negative.
Expand a bracket by multiplying every term inside it; solve an equation using the same reversible operation on both sides, checking any division is allowed.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · M4.1, M4.3, M4.4, M4.8

example.question: Find \(2a^2-3b\) when \(a=-2\) and \(b=3\).
steps: Substitute with brackets: \(2(-2)^2-3(3)\).
Evaluate the square first: \(2(4)-9=8-9\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: \((-2)^2=4\), but \(-2^2=-(2^2)=-4\); brackets change what is squared.

additionalConcepts.title: Convert fractions, decimals and percentages
knowledge: Write a terminating decimal over the appropriate power of ten and simplify; divide the numerator by the denominator to turn a fraction into a decimal.
A percentage means parts per hundred, so \(p\%=p/100\); these are equivalent ways to represent the same quantity.
For a recurring decimal, name the value and multiply by powers of ten until two copies have the same repeating tail.
Subtract those copies to remove the repeating tail, then solve the resulting equation and simplify the fraction.
A fraction in lowest terms has a terminating decimal exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5; otherwise its decimal eventually repeats.

example.question: Convert \(0.1\overline{6}=0.1666\ldots\) to a fraction.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Do not replace a recurring decimal by a rounded terminating one: \(0.1667\ne\tfrac16\).

additionalConcepts.title: Use prime factors to find HCF and LCM
knowledge: A prime is an integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Every integer greater than 1 has a unique product of prime factors, apart from their order; repeated factors can be written as powers.
A factor divides a number exactly, and a multiple is an integer times that number; divisibility can be checked by comparing prime-factor exponents.
The highest common factor uses the smallest exponent of each shared prime, while the lowest common multiple uses the largest exponent of every prime present.
For positive integers \(a,b\), \(\operatorname{HCF}(a,b)\operatorname{LCM}(a,b)=ab\).

example.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 120.
steps: Factorise: \(72=2^3\times3^2\) and \(120=2^3\times3\times5\).
Take shared minimum powers: \(\operatorname{HCF}=2^3\times3=24\).
Take all maximum powers: \(\operatorname{LCM}=2^3\times3^2\times5=360\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A common multiple must contain enough copies of every required prime; being divisible by each distinct prime once is not sufficient.

additionalConcepts.title: Draw regions for two-variable inequalities
knowledge: Replace a linear inequality by equality to draw its straight boundary line.
Use a solid boundary for \(\le\) or \(\ge\), and a dashed boundary for strict \(<\) or \(>\).
Test a point away from the boundary to identify the permitted half-plane; inequalities such as \(y>mx+c\) select points above the line.
An AND requires the overlap of the permitted regions, while an OR permits points in either region.
A point on an excluded boundary fails that inequality even if it satisfies every other condition.

example.question: Describe the region satisfying \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge1\) and \(x+y<4\).
steps: Draw solid lines \(x=0\) and \(y=1\), and a dashed line \(y=4-x\).
Keep points to the right of \(x=0\), above \(y=1\), and below \(y=4-x\).
The sloping boundary meets \(y=1\) at \(x=3\), so the allowed horizontal range is \(0\le x<3\).
example.answer: \(0\le x<3\) and \(1\le y<4-x\); the point \((0,1)\) is included and the sloping edge is excluded.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: For simultaneous inequalities, retain the overlap of all regions, not everything shaded by any one condition.

additionalConcepts.title: Find a quadratic sequence’s nth term
knowledge: A linear sequence has constant first differences and can be written \(u_n=an+b\).
A quadratic sequence has constant nonzero second differences and can be written \(u_n=an^2+bn+c\).
The second difference is \(2a\), so halve it to find the coefficient of \(n^2\).
Subtract \(an^2\) from each given term; the remaining linear sequence determines \(b\) and \(c\).
Check the resulting formula against the supplied terms and use the stated starting index.

example.question: A sequence begins \(3,8,15,24\) and has a quadratic nth term, starting at \(n=1\). Find it.
steps: The first differences are \(5,7,9\), so the second differences are \(2,2\), giving \(a=1\).
This remainder is \(2n\), so \(u_n=n^2+2n\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: The second difference is twice the quadratic coefficient, and a short list alone does not prove the generating rule is quadratic.

additionalConcepts.title: Read motion from gradients and areas
knowledge: The gradient of a distance-travelled–time graph is speed; the gradient of a displacement–time graph is velocity, which may be negative.
A horizontal distance–time segment means no distance is being added, and a steeper segment means greater speed.
The gradient of a speed–time graph gives the rate of change of speed; the gradient of a velocity–time graph gives signed acceleration.
The area under a speed–time graph is distance travelled; signed area under a velocity–time graph is displacement, so split and use absolute areas for total distance.
Gradient units are vertical-axis units divided by horizontal-axis units, and area units are their product; convert units consistently before calculating.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · M1.1, M1.2, M4.13, M4.14, MM6.1

example.question: A speed–time graph rises in a straight line from \(0\,\mathrm{m/s}\) at \(0\,\mathrm{s}\) to \(6\,\mathrm{m/s}\) at \(4\,\mathrm{s}\), then stays at 6 m/s until 10 s. Find the initial acceleration and total distance.
steps: The initial gradient is \((6-0)/(4-0)=1.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\).
The first area is a triangle: \(\tfrac12\times4\times6=12\,\mathrm{m}\).
The remaining area is a rectangle: \((10-4)\times6=36\,\mathrm{m}\); total distance is \(12+36=48\,\mathrm{m}\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: The height of a speed–time graph is speed, not distance; distance comes from the area.

additionalConcepts.title: Estimate rates and totals from scaled graphs
knowledge: To estimate an instantaneous rate from a curve, draw a tangent at the required point and find its gradient.
Choose two well-separated points on the tangent and calculate change in vertical value divided by change in horizontal value using the axis scales.
A chord between two curve points gives an average rate over an interval, which can differ from the tangent rate at one instant.
Estimate an area by splitting it into rectangles, triangles or trapezia; for one trapezium use \(\tfrac12\times\text{width}\times(\text{first height}+\text{last height})\).
Interpret the estimate in context: a cost–time gradient has units of money per time, while an area under a pay-rate–time graph represents money.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · M4.13, M4.14, MM6.1, MM7.5

example.question: A tangent to a cost–time curve at 5 hours passes through the plotted points \((2,30)\) and \((8,90)\), with cost in pounds. Estimate the rate at 5 hours.
steps: Use the two points on the tangent: the cost change is \(90-30=60\) pounds.
The time change is \(8-2=6\) hours.
The tangent gradient is approximately \(60/6=10\) pounds per hour.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Use points on the tangent and the numerical axis scales; the curve’s height or the tangent’s visual angle is not the rate.

additionalConcepts.title: Estimate equation solutions from intersections
knowledge: The solutions of \(f(x)=0\) are the x-coordinates where the graph meets the x-axis.
The solutions of \(f(x)=g(x)\) are the x-coordinates of intersections of \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=g(x)\).
For simultaneous equations, report both coordinates of each intersection, since both equations must hold at the same point.
Read each scale carefully, interpolate between marked values, and give only the accuracy supported by the graph.
Check the whole permitted interval for further intersections; touching a curve also gives a solution.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · M4.13, M4.15, M4.16, MM8.7

example.question: To solve \(x^2+x-1=0\), a scaled graph of \(y=x^2\) and \(y=1-x\) shows intersections at approximately \((-1.62,2.62)\) and \((0.62,0.38)\). Give the roots to 1 decimal place.
steps: Rearrange the equation as \(x^2=1-x\), so these graph intersections correspond to its solutions.
Read their x-coordinates: approximately \(-1.62\) and \(0.62\).
Round each x-coordinate to one decimal place.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: An equation in x asks for intersection x-coordinates; do not substitute the intersection heights as the roots.

additionalConcepts.title: Recognise exponential and logarithmic graphs
knowledge: For \(a>0\), the graph of \(y=a^x\) has positive outputs and passes through \((0,1)\) and \((1,a)\).
For \(a>1\) the exponential increases, while for \(0<a<1\) it decreases; in each case \(y=0\) is a horizontal asymptote, whereas \(a=1\) gives the constant graph \(y=1\).
For \(a>0\) and \(a\ne1\), \(y=\log_a x\) has domain \(x>0\), passes through \((1,0)\) and \((a,1)\), and has vertical asymptote \(x=0\).
A logarithm increases for \(a>1\) and decreases for \(0<a<1\), so applying a decreasing logarithm reverses an inequality.
The graphs of \(y=a^x\) and \(y=\log_a x\) are reflections in \(y=x\) because their inputs and outputs are interchanged.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · MM5.1, MM5.2, MM8.1, M4.12

example.question: Which standard exponential or logarithmic graph has domain \(x>0\), decreases, passes through \((1,0)\) and \((\tfrac12,1)\), and has vertical asymptote \(x=0\)?
steps: The domain and vertical asymptote match a logarithm, rather than an exponential.
For \(y=\log_a x\), the point \((a,1)\) identifies the base, giving \(a=\tfrac12\).
The base lies between 0 and 1, consistent with the graph decreasing.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A positive exponential base does not always give an increasing graph; bases between 0 and 1 reverse the direction.

additionalConcepts.title: Recognise square-root and reciprocal graphs
knowledge: The graph of \(y=\sqrt{x}\) starts at \((0,0)\), has domain and range \([0,\infty)\), and passes through \((1,1)\), \((4,2)\) and \((9,3)\).
The square-root graph increases and becomes less steep; it is the reflection of the \(x\ge0\) half of \(y=x^2\) in \(y=x\).
The graph of \(y=1/x\) has domain \(x\ne0\), range \(y\ne0\), and the two axes as asymptotes.
The reciprocal graph has branches in the first and third quadrants and decreases on each side of zero; it never joins across the excluded input.
Use key points, domains and asymptotes together, then apply any stated translations, stretches or reflections.

example.question: For \(y=1/(x-2)+1\), find the asymptotes and the intercepts with the coordinate axes.
steps: Translating \(y=1/x\) two units right and one up gives asymptotes \(x=2\) and \(y=1\).
For the y-intercept set \(x=0\): \(y=-1/2+1=1/2\).
For the x-intercept set \(y=0\): \(1/(x-2)=-1\), hence \(x=1\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: For a square-root graph retain only the nonnegative root; for a reciprocal graph retain its excluded input.

additionalConcepts.title: Find line equations and compare gradients
knowledge: A point \((x,y)\) gives horizontal position first and vertical position second; the signs place it in one of the four quadrants.
For two points with different x-coordinates, the gradient is \(m=(y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1)\); a line through \((x_1,y_1)\) is \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\).
In \(y=mx+c\), \(m\) sets the gradient and \(c\) the y-intercept; a line may also be written \(ax+by+c=0\).
Distinct nonvertical parallel lines have equal gradients, and perpendicular lines with finite nonzero gradients satisfy \(m_1m_2=-1\).
Vertical lines have form \(x=k\) and no finite gradient; horizontal lines have gradient zero, and these two directions are perpendicular.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · MM3.1, MM8.3, M4.9, M4.10

example.question: Find the line through \((2,-1)\) parallel to \(3x-2y+4=0\).
steps: Rearrange the given line: \(y=\tfrac32x+2\), so its gradient is \(3/2\).
Use the same gradient through the given point: \(y+1=\tfrac32(x-2)\).
Expand and rearrange: \(y=\tfrac32x-4\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Parallel lines share a gradient; they need not share an intercept. Use a negative reciprocal only for perpendicular lines.

additionalConcepts.title: Give each allowed input exactly one output
knowledge: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain; different inputs may share the same output.
A one-to-one function has different outputs for different inputs, while a many-to-one function repeats at least one output.
A graph represents a function of x only if each vertical line meets it at most once, with every allowed input assigned a value.
The notation \(\sqrt{x}\) means the nonnegative square root: \(\sqrt9=3\), although solving \(u^2=9\) gives \(u=\pm3\).
The modulus \(|x|\) is distance from zero, so it equals \(x\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(-x\) for \(x<0\); in particular \(\sqrt{x^2}=|x|\).

example.question: Does \(y^2=x\) define y as a function of x on \(x\ge0\)? What changes for \(y=\sqrt{x}\)?
steps: At \(x=4\), the relation \(y^2=x\) allows both \(y=2\) and \(y=-2\).
One allowed input has two outputs, so this relation does not define a function of x.
The rule \(y=\sqrt{x}\) selects only the nonnegative output, giving exactly one output for each \(x\ge0\).
example.answer: \(y^2=x\) is not a function of x on this domain; \(y=\sqrt{x}\) is.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Many inputs giving one output is allowed; one input giving several outputs is not a function.

additionalConcepts.title: Name geometric objects and recognise symmetry
knowledge: A point records a location, a line extends in both directions, a line segment has two endpoints, and a plane is a flat surface extending in all directions.
A vertex is a corner; an edge is where faces of a solid meet, while the sides of a polygon are line segments.
Parallel lines in a plane never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, and the middle letter of \(\angle ABC\) names its vertex \(B\).
The angle subtended by segment \(AB\) at \(C\) is \(\angle ACB\); a polygon is a closed plane figure with straight sides, and a regular polygon has equal sides and equal interior angles.

A line of symmetry reflects a shape onto itself; rotational symmetry of order \(k\) gives \(k\) matching positions in one full turn, and a regular \(n\)-gon has \(n\) symmetry lines and rotational order \(n\).

example.question: A regular hexagon is rotated about its centre: what is the smallest positive angle that makes it coincide with itself, and how many lines of symmetry does it have?
steps: Its six equally spaced vertices divide a full turn into six equal turns.
The smallest turn is \(360^\circ/6=60^\circ\).
Three symmetry lines join opposite vertices and three join midpoints of opposite sides.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Equal side lengths alone do not make a polygon regular: its interior angles must also be equal.

additionalConcepts.title: Use angle facts, parallel lines and polygon sums
knowledge: Angles around a point total \(360^\circ\), angles on a straight line total \(180^\circ\), and perpendicular lines form \(90^\circ\) angles.
Vertically opposite angles at the intersection of two straight lines are equal.
When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles total \(180^\circ\).
A triangle has interior-angle sum \(180^\circ\), a quadrilateral has sum \(360^\circ\), and a triangle’s exterior angle equals the sum of its two opposite interior angles.

A simple \(n\)-sided polygon has interior-angle sum \((n-2)180^\circ\); the exterior turning angles of a convex polygon total \(360^\circ\), so a regular polygon has exterior angle \(360^\circ/n\) and interior angle \(180^\circ-360^\circ/n\).

example.question: A regular polygon has interior angle \(150^\circ\); how many sides does it have?
steps: An interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle lie on a straight line, so the exterior angle is \(180^\circ-150^\circ=30^\circ\).
The exterior angles total \(360^\circ\), and all are equal because the polygon is regular.
The number of sides is \(360/30=12\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Equal corresponding or alternate angles require parallel lines; a diagram that merely looks parallel is not enough.

additionalConcepts.title: Use the defining properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
knowledge: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three \(60^\circ\) angles, an isosceles triangle has two equal sides with equal opposite angles, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides; acute, right-angled and obtuse describe its angles.
A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal, opposite angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary, and diagonals that bisect each other.

A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles and equal diagonals; a rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides, perpendicular diagonals and diagonals that bisect its angles; a square has both sets of properties.
A trapezium has a pair of parallel opposite sides; an isosceles trapezium has equal nonparallel sides and equal base angles, but a general trapezium need not have those extra properties.

A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides, and the diagonal joining the vertices where those equal pairs meet is a symmetry line that perpendicularly bisects the other diagonal; derive needed side and angle facts by drawing a diagonal and using triangles.

example.question: In parallelogram \(ABCD\), the vertices are in order and \(\angle DAB=68^\circ\); find the other three interior angles.
steps: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so \(\angle BCD=68^\circ\).
Adjacent angles are supplementary because opposite sides are parallel, so \(\angle ABC=180^\circ-68^\circ=112^\circ\).
The remaining opposite pair gives \(\angle CDA=112^\circ\); the four angles total \(360^\circ\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A rhombus need not have right angles, and a rectangle need not have four equal sides; perpendicular diagonals alone do not force a square.

additionalConcepts.title: Prove triangles congruent with SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS
knowledge: Congruent triangles have the same size and shape, so their corresponding sides and angles are equal even when one triangle is reflected or rotated.
SSS requires three equal corresponding side pairs, while SAS requires two equal corresponding side pairs and the equal angle between them.
ASA requires two equal corresponding angle pairs and the equal included side; if a different corresponding side is given, use the triangle angle sum to obtain the included-angle version.
RHS requires both triangles to be right-angled, equal hypotenuses and one equal pair of other sides.
Write the vertex correspondence carefully and name the criterion before using equality of any remaining sides or angles.

example.question: In quadrilateral \(ABCD\), \(AB=AD\) and \(BC=DC\); prove \(\angle ABC=\angle ADC\).
steps: Draw diagonal \(AC\), giving triangles \(ABC\) and \(ADC\).
The corresponding side pairs are \(AB=AD\), \(BC=DC\), and the shared side \(AC=AC\).
The triangles are congruent by SSS, with \(B\) corresponding to \(D\), so their corresponding angles \(\angle ABC\) and \(\angle ADC\) are equal.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: AAA establishes similarity rather than congruence, and two sides with a non-included angle do not generally establish congruence.

additionalConcepts.title: Label the sides before using right-triangle ratios
knowledge: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; opposite and adjacent are named relative to the chosen acute angle \(\theta\), with adjacent excluding the hypotenuse.
The ratios are \(\sin\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse}\), \(\cos\theta=\text{adjacent}/\text{hypotenuse}\), and \(\tan\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{adjacent}\).
Pythagoras gives \(a^2+b^2=c^2\) when \(c\) is the hypotenuse; rearrange a ratio to find a length or identify an angle from its known exact ratio.
For a general triangle, a perpendicular height can create right triangles; in three dimensions, select the correct face, cross-section or projection before applying the same rules.

example.question: A right-angled triangle has sides of length \(6\), \(8\) and \(10\), with \(\theta\) opposite the side of length \(6\); find \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\).
steps: The hypotenuse is \(10\), and \(6^2+8^2=10^2\) confirms the right triangle.
Relative to \(\theta\), the opposite side is \(6\) and the adjacent side is \(8\).
Therefore \(\sin\theta=6/10\), \(\cos\theta=8/10\), and \(\tan\theta=6/8\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Opposite and adjacent swap when you change the chosen acute angle; the hypotenuse never changes.

additionalConcepts.title: Compare observed frequencies with expected outcomes
knowledge: A probability lies between \(0\) and \(1\): impossible events have probability \(0\), certain events have probability \(1\), and a fair model assigns equal probabilities to its equally likely elementary outcomes.
Record experimental counts in a frequency table or frequency tree, checking that every node’s child counts add to its total and that each result is counted once.
Relative frequency is \(\text{event count}/\text{trial count}\), an estimate of the event’s probability; it can differ from the theoretical value because trials are random.
For \(N\) future trials with the same probability \(p\) of success on each trial, the expected frequency is \(Np\) and the relative expected frequency is \(p\).

An expected frequency is a long-run average prediction, not a guaranteed count; for independent trials with the same success probability, a larger trial count generally gives a more stable relative-frequency estimate.

example.question: Fifty pairs of fair-coin tosses give \(HH:14\), \(HT:12\), \(TH:11\), \(TT:13\); organise the counts and compare the observed proportion of two heads with the theoretical expected number in \(300\) further pairs.
steps: The frequency tree is \(\begin{array}{ccccccc}&&&50&&&\\&&\swarrow&&\searrow&&\\&H:26&&&&T:24&\\\swarrow&&\searrow&&\swarrow&&\searrow\\HH:14&&HT:12&&TH:11&&TT:13\end{array}\); counts leaving each branch add to its parent total.

The matching table is \(\begin{array}{c|rr|r}\text{First/second}&H&T&\text{Total}\\\hline H&14&12&26\\T&11&13&24\\\hline\text{Total}&25&25&50\end{array}\), so the observed relative frequency of \(HH\) is \(14/50=0.28\).
The four ordered outcomes are equally likely for two independent fair tosses, so the theoretical probability of \(HH\) is \(1/4=0.25\).
The theoretical expected number in \(300\) future pairs is \(300/4=75\); using the observed estimate instead gives \(300(0.28)=84\), and neither is a guaranteed actual count.
example.answer: Observed relative frequency \(0.28\); theoretical probability \(0.25\); theoretical expected frequency \(75\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Do not infer that a coin is unfair from one unequal batch or treat an expected count as a promise about the next batch.

additionalConcepts.title: Add disjoint outcomes and use complements
knowledge: Elementary outcomes are exhaustive when together they cover every possibility, and their probabilities sum to \(1\).
Events are mutually exclusive when they cannot both happen in the same trial; add their probabilities to find the probability that one of them happens.
If mutually exclusive events are also exhaustive, their probabilities sum to \(1\), so a missing probability is one minus the sum of the others.
The complement of an event is everything outside it, giving \(P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)\); an exhaustive list of overlapping events must not be added without correcting for double counting.

example.question: A spinner lands on exactly one of red, blue or green, with probabilities \(2/5\), \(1/4\) and \(g\); find \(g\) and the probability of not landing on blue.
steps: The three colours are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so \(2/5+1/4+g=1\).
Not blue is the complement of blue, giving \(1-1/4=3/4\); equivalently, add red and green: \(8/20+7/20=15/20\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: “Exhaustive” alone does not permit adding event probabilities to get one: the events must also be mutually exclusive.

additionalConcepts.title: List equally likely outcomes in a sample-space grid
knowledge: A possibility space lists every elementary outcome exactly once; systematic lists, tables and grids help prevent omissions and repeated counting.
For a single experiment with equally likely outcomes, \(P(A)=\text{number of favourable outcomes}/\text{total number of outcomes}\).
For two combined experiments, label the rows by the first result and columns by the second, then put the corresponding ordered pair or requested value in each cell.
Independent fair selections make the ordered cells equally likely, but repeated totals can occupy several cells and are therefore not necessarily equally likely.
Use a tree or appropriately weighted counts when the elementary outcomes are not equally likely instead of dividing unweighted counts.

example.question: Two independent fair spinners each show \(1\), \(2\) or \(3\); use a grid to find the probability that their total is \(4\).
steps: Put the first spinner on rows and the second on columns: \(\begin{array}{c|ccc}+&1&2&3\\\hline1&2&3&4\\2&3&4&5\\3&4&5&6\end{array}\).
There are \(3\times3=9\) equally likely ordered outcomes.
Total \(4\) occurs in the three cells \((1,3)\), \((2,2)\), \((3,1)\), giving probability \(3/9=1/3\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: The totals \(2,3,4,5,6\) are not equally likely, so counting one successful total out of five gives the wrong answer.

additionalConcepts.title: Follow conditional probabilities along a tree
knowledge: A probability tree branches at each stage, and the probabilities on branches leaving any one node sum to \(1\).
Each later branch probability is conditional on the earlier outcomes along that route, so multiply branch probabilities along a route to find its joint probability.
Add the probabilities of distinct complete routes that satisfy the requested event, since a trial follows only one complete route.
For independent trials, the next-stage probabilities do not change with earlier outcomes; without replacement, update both the remaining favourable count and the remaining total.
Choose a convenient starting total when drawing an expected-frequency tree, multiply it along the branches, and divide relevant end counts by the total of the group being conditioned on.

example.question: A bag contains \(3\) red balls and \(2\) blue balls; two balls are drawn without replacement, so use a tree to find the probability of exactly one red ball.
steps: The tree is \(\begin{array}{ccccccc}&&&\text{Start}&&&\\&&\swarrow&&\searrow&&\\&R:3/5&&&&B:2/5&\\\swarrow&&\searrow&&\swarrow&&\searrow\\R:2/4&&B:2/4&&R:3/4&&B:1/4\end{array}\); the labels at the second stage are conditional probabilities after the first draw.
Exactly one red means \(RB\) or \(BR\), so add their probabilities: \(3/10+3/10=3/5\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Do not keep the original second-draw probabilities after removing a ball, and do not multiply the two alternative routes together.

additionalConcepts.title: Use Venn regions and two-way tables for conditional probability
knowledge: A Venn diagram divides a population into disjoint regions such as both groups, the first only, the second only, and neither; place the overlap first so it is counted once.
A two-way table records the same information by cross-classifying two yes/no properties, and its row and column totals identify the relevant groups.
To calculate a conditional probability, restrict the denominator to the given group and count the desired outcomes inside that group.
To find an inclusive “or” probability, add the relevant disjoint regions, or add the two group totals and subtract the overlap once.
When given probabilities rather than actual counts, scale them to a convenient common expected total and use the same table or Venn-region method.

example.question: Of \(100\) students, \(40\) play chess, \(30\) play music, and \(10\) do both; fill the Venn regions and a two-way table, then find the probability that a randomly chosen music player also plays chess.
steps: The Venn regions are both \(10\), chess only \(40-10=30\), music only \(30-10=20\), and neither \(100-10-30-20=40\).
The table is \(\begin{array}{c|rr|r}&\text{Music}&\text{No music}&\text{Total}\\\hline\text{Chess}&10&30&40\\\text{No chess}&20&40&60\\\hline\text{Total}&30&70&100\end{array}\).
Conditioning on music restricts the choice to its \(30\) players; \(10\) of those also play chess, so the probability is \(10/30=1/3\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: The denominator is the \(30\) music players, not all \(100\) students; reversing the condition would change the denominator to \(40\).

additionalConcepts.title: Match corresponding sides in similar triangles
knowledge: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and one common positive scale factor between corresponding side lengths.
Two equal angle pairs establish triangle similarity because the third angles must also agree. Name the correspondence before writing ratios.
Parallel lines often create equal corresponding or alternate angles and therefore similar triangles; justify those angles before using a scale factor.
For corresponding length ratio \(k\), similar figures have area ratio \(k^2\), and similar solids have volume ratio \(k^3\).
Equal area alone does not make triangles similar. Conversely, similar triangles of equal positive area have scale factor one and are congruent.

references.label: TMUA specification: M3.10, M5.5 and M5.17

example.question: In triangle ABC, P lies on AB and Q lies on AC, with PQ parallel to BC. Given \(AP=4\), \(AB=10\) and \(AC=15\), find AQ and the ratio of the areas of APQ and ABC.
steps: The parallel lines give equal corresponding angles, so triangles APQ and ABC are similar, with A matching A, P matching B and Q matching C.
The length scale from ABC to APQ is \(AP/AB=4/10=2/5\). Thus \(AQ=(2/5)\times15=6\).
The area ratio is the square of the length ratio: \((2/5)^2=4/25\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Keep corresponding sides in the same order in every ratio. A length scale factor is squared for area, not used unchanged.

additionalConcepts.title: Solve two equations together
knowledge: A solution of simultaneous equations must satisfy both equations for the same values of the unknowns.
For two linear equations, multiply and add or subtract them to eliminate one variable, or rearrange one equation and substitute into the other.
For a line and a quadratic curve, isolate one variable using the line, then substitute that entire expression into the curve equation.
Solve the resulting quadratic, keeping every allowed root. Substitute each root into the line to recover its paired coordinate.
Check every pair in both original equations. A line and a quadratic curve may have two, one or no real intersections.

example.question: Solve simultaneously \(x+y=5\) and \(y=x^2-1\).
steps: The linear equation gives \(y=5-x\). Both expressions for \(y\) must agree, so \(5-x=x^2-1\).
Rearrange and factor: \(x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)=0\). Hence \(x=-3\) or \(x=2\).
Use \(y=5-x\) separately for each root: \(x=-3\) gives \(y=8\), while \(x=2\) gives \(y=3\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Do not pair the x-value from one root with the y-value from the other. Each intersection is a complete ordered pair.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification: MM1.4 and M4.15, simultaneous equations

additionalConcepts.title: Count polynomial roots from signs and degree
knowledge: A polynomial graph is continuous. If its values at two inputs have opposite signs, it must cross the horizontal axis at least once between them.
Values of the same sign do not rule out roots between them: the graph may cross twice or touch the axis. Check separately whether an endpoint itself is a root.
A nonzero polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) distinct real roots. A repeated root counts only once when the question asks for distinct roots.
For sufficiently large positive or negative inputs, the leading term determines the sign. Use its coefficient and whether its degree is odd or even to establish the two tails.
Find disjoint intervals that each contain a root, then compare this lower bound with the degree's upper bound. When these bounds agree, the root count is exact.

example.question: Show that \(f(x)=x^3-4x\) has exactly three distinct real roots by considering signs and degree.
steps: There is a sign change on each of \((-3,-1)\), \((-1,1)\) and \((1,3)\). Continuity gives at least one root in each of these disjoint intervals, so at least three distinct roots.
The polynomial is a nonzero cubic, so it has at most three distinct real roots. Therefore it has exactly three.
As a check, \(x^3-4x=x(x-2)(x+2)\), giving the three roots \(-2,0,2\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A sign change proves at least one root, not exactly one. Do not conclude there are no roots between two values of the same sign.

additionalConcepts.title: Estimate calculations containing pi and square roots
knowledge: For a rough estimate, replace quantities by nearby numbers that make the arithmetic simple. Write \(\approx\) rather than claiming exact equality.
Choose an approximation to \(\pi\) to suit the task: \(3\) can give a rough scale check, while \(3.14\) gives a closer numerical estimate. Neither is an exact replacement.
Estimate a positive square root using nearby squares. Since \(2.2^2=4.84<5<5.29=2.3^2\), we have \(2.2<\sqrt{5}<2.3\).
Apply the arithmetic to the approximated quantities, retaining brackets, powers and units. Distinguish a rough estimate from a justified upper or lower bound.
Keep \(\pi\) and surds exact when the question asks for an exact result; approximate only to estimate or check size.

example.question: Give a rough estimate of \(\frac{4\pi\sqrt{15}}{1.98}\) using simple nearby numbers.
steps: Use \(\pi\approx3\), \(\sqrt{15}\approx4\) because \(16=4^2\), and \(1.98\approx2\).
Substitute the approximations: \(\frac{4\pi\sqrt{15}}{1.98}\approx\frac{4\times3\times4}{2}\).
Calculate \(4\times3\times4\div2=24\). This is a rough estimate, not an exact value or a proved bound.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A rounded numerator and denominator can change a quotient in different directions. A rough estimate alone does not establish an upper or lower bound.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification: M2.14, estimation including pi and surds

additionalConcepts.title: Use all four operations with algebraic fractions
knowledge: Before simplifying, exclude every value that makes an original denominator zero. When dividing by a fraction, also exclude every value that makes the divisor zero.
To add or subtract fractions, use a common denominator. For nonzero denominators, \(\frac{A}{B}\pm\frac{C}{D}=\frac{AD\pm BC}{BD}\); factor first to find a smaller common denominator when possible.
To multiply fractions, multiply numerators and denominators: \(\frac{A}{B}\times\frac{C}{D}=\frac{AC}{BD}\). Factor before cancelling.

To divide by a nonzero fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: \( rac{A}{B}\div rac{C}{D}= rac{AD}{BC}\), with \(B
e0\), \(D
e0\) and \(C
e0\).
Cancel complete common factors, never individual terms across addition or subtraction. Keep original exclusions even when the simplified expression is defined there.

example.question: Let \(A=\frac{2}{x-1}\) and \(B=\frac{1}{x+1}\). Simplify \(A+B\), \(A-B\), \(AB\) and \(A\div B\), stating their domains.
steps: Both original fractions require \(x\ne1\) and \(x\ne-1\). On this domain \(B\) is never zero, so division adds no further exclusion.
For subtraction, retain the numerator bracket: \(A-B=\frac{2(x+1)-(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{x+3}{x^2-1}\).
Multiply corresponding numerators and denominators: \(AB=\frac{2}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{2}{x^2-1}\).
Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal: \(A\div B=\frac{2}{x-1}\times\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{2(x+1)}{x-1}\). The original exclusion \(x=-1\) still applies.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: When subtracting, subtract the whole adjusted numerator. When dividing, the divisor itself must be nonzero as well as defined.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification: M4.6, algebraic rational expressions
